checkpoints: Canary strategy ramps traffic in 3 steps via setWeight: 20% → 50% → 100%

Each pause below 100% has a concrete duration (e.g. 5m) instead of an empty pause — an empty pause waits indefinitely for manual promotion, which contradicts the requirement to wait automatically on a timer
An analysis step immediately follows each pause below 100%, referencing a separate AnalysisTemplate rather than inlining the metric check
The analysis step is deliberately omitted at the final 100% step, since there is no canary traffic left to compare against once the rollout is fully promoted

The AnalysisTemplate's Prometheus query filters by rollouts_pod_template_hash in both the numerator and the denominator, so it measures only the canary's traffic and never mixes it with stable traffic
failureLimit: 2 combined with the analysis interval means it takes 2 consecutive readings that breach the error-rate successCondition before the AnalysisRun is marked Failed
A Failed AnalysisRun drives the Rollout to auto-abort back to stable with no manual intervention

Default GitLab pipelines run by sequential stages: every job in a stage (e.g. `test`) must fully finish before the next stage (e.g. `deploy`) starts, regardless of whether `deploy` actually depends on all of those jobs.
This causes pointless blocking: an unrelated slow job in the `test` stage (e.g. lint) still delays `deploy` even though `deploy` only needs the result of one specific job in that stage.
The mechanism that actually solves this is `needs`: declaring `deploy: needs: [test_integration]` turns the pipeline into a DAG (directed acyclic graph).
With `needs`, the `deploy` job starts as soon as `test_integration` finishes, without waiting for other jobs also in the `test` stage to complete.
The `stage` field is still kept on `deploy` (e.g. `stage: deploy`) — GitLab still uses it to display the pipeline in columns on the UI and to validate structure.
Once `needs` is declared, `stage` no longer decides the actual run order — the run order is determined by job dependencies instead.
Because of this, two jobs declared under the same stage can run out of phase (not together) if one of them has a `needs` pointing to an earlier dependency than the other.

The real benefit is that total pipeline time drops significantly when jobs are not truly sequentially dependent, since each job runs as soon as its real dependency is met instead of waiting on the whole stage.
Root cause: identifies that Recreate stops all old Pods before any new one starts, leaving a window where zero Pods are serving — that gap is what produces the 502s.
Rolling update's fix mechanism: explains Pods are swapped gradually in small batches so at least some Pods are always serving, which removes the downtime-caused 502s.

Directly answers the manager's yes/no framing with a qualified stance: rolling update fixes the downtime problem, but that alone doesn't mean everything is safe — more must be covered before calling it "done".

Limit 1 (slow rollback): if the new version turns out buggy, rolling back happens gradually pod-by-pod (not an instant switch like blue-green), so users keep hitting the broken version during that time.
Limit 2 (no observation phase): rolling update ramps to 100% traffic as soon as the rollout finishes, with no small-slice canary-style observation window beforehand to check real error rate/latency.

Consequence of the missing observation phase: a non-crashing logic bug (wrong results, not a crash) can already be hitting every user before anyone notices via metrics, since there was no gated ramp-up to catch it early.

Limit 3 (mixed-version risk): old and new Pods serve requests in parallel during the rollout, so a non-backward-compatible API/schema change can cause requests to fail depending on which version randomly handles them.
Names blue-green and/or canary specifically as what needs to be layered on top of rolling update to get instant rollback and/or a pre-ramp traffic observation window.
Not the same mechanism for both — `artifacts` and `cache` serve two different purposes.
`artifacts` passes data BETWEEN JOBS within the same pipeline run: a later job (via `needs`/later stage) is guaranteed to get exactly the previous job's output from this run.
Artifacts are also downloadable from the GitLab UI for inspection.
`cache` reuses data ACROSS DIFFERENT pipeline runs to speed things up (avoid reinstalling from scratch every run).
Cache does not guarantee the data is exactly right for this run — it could be a stale copy from a previous run if not yet invalidated.

For `dist/`: use `artifacts` on the `build` job, because `deploy` needs exactly this run's build output; using `cache` here risks `deploy` receiving a stale `dist/` and deploying the wrong artifact, a hard-to-spot bug.

For `node_modules/`: use `cache` with a key tied to the lockfile (`cache: key: files: [package-lock.json]`), since the goal is avoiding a full `npm install` when dependencies haven't changed, with no need for the exactly-once guarantee of an artifact, and the cache self-invalidates when the lockfile/key changes.

If swapped, using `artifacts` for `node_modules/` means every new pipeline run still has to reinstall from scratch, since artifacts don't carry over to a different run — losing the speed benefit cache provides.

Nhận diện đúng vấn đề ngay từ đầu: đây không phải "job đã chạy và fail" mà là job `deploy_prod` hoàn toàn vắng mặt khỏi danh sách job của pipeline (không nằm trong failed lẫn skipped) — dấu hiệu cho thấy `rules` chưa từng tạo ra job này; đây cũng chính là thông điệp mấu chốt cần truyền đạt lại cho team (hai loại vấn đề khác nhau, đòi hỏi cách debug khác nhau).
Nắm đúng cơ chế cốt lõi: `rules` quyết định một job có được TẠO RA cho pipeline cụ thể này hay không, đây là điều hoàn toàn khác với việc job đã chạy rồi pass/fail.

Giả thuyết 1 (tác nhân kỹ thuật): nếu pipeline chạy dưới dạng merge request pipeline (do team bật `only: [merge_requests]` toàn cục hoặc dựa vào workflow rules mặc định của GitLab), `$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH` có thể RỖNG trong ngữ cảnh đó, biến đúng phải dùng là `$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_TARGET_BRANCH_NAME`.
Giả thuyết 1 (hệ quả): suy ra chuỗi nhân-quả — điều kiện `if` không bao giờ khớp → job không được tạo → pipeline vẫn hiện "green" vì GitLab không tính một job không tồn tại là failure.
Giả thuyết 2 (tác nhân kỹ thuật): nếu pipeline chạy như một branch pipeline bình thường trên `main` (điều kiện khớp), job SẼ được tạo ra, nhưng ở trạng thái chờ-bấm do `when: manual`.
Giả thuyết 2 (hệ quả): nếu không ai chủ động bấm nút play trên UI, job cứ nằm ở trạng thái "manual, chưa chạy", và toàn bộ pipeline vẫn có thể báo passed tùy theo cấu hình `allow_failure`.

Bước xác nhận cụ thể để chọn giữa 2 giả thuyết: kiểm tra loại pipeline (branch vs merge request) qua UI hoặc biến `CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE`, rồi đối chiếu xem `$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH` thực sự mang giá trị gì trong ngữ cảnh đó.

DEPLOY_TOKEN's value is hardcoded directly in HCL (value = "abc"), which is a security issue because it lands in git history and Terraform state — the same class of mistake as hardcoding credentials in Jenkins.
That hardcoded value is also too short/invalid to satisfy GitLab's masking requirements — a maskable value needs sufficient length, no whitespace, and to be base64-friendly.

Because the value fails those masking requirements, setting masked = true on it will make GitLab either reject the variable creation with a validation error, or accept it but fail to actually mask it in pipeline logs.

Fix: DEPLOY_TOKEN should be read from a Terraform variable injected via TF_VAR_deploy_token, the same way registry_password already does it correctly, using a real token value long enough to be maskable (e.g. a glpat-... token).
Second issue: neither resource sets protected = true for these deploy secrets — DEPLOY_TOKEN explicitly sets protected = false, and REGISTRY_PASSWORD leaves it unset, so it also defaults to false.
Consequence: protected = false means every pipeline — even one running on an arbitrary feature/MR branch — can read the production deploy secret, widening the exposure far beyond where it should be.
Fix: set protected = true on both resources so the secrets are only readable by pipelines running on a protected branch/tag (e.g. main or a release tag), shrinking the risk surface accordingly.
Identifies the root cause: `key: build` is a fixed string not tied to branch or dependency content, so every branch shares the exact same `node_modules/` cache.
Explains the trigger: when branch B removes a package from its `package-lock.json` and runs `npm ci`, the resulting `node_modules/` (missing that package) overwrites the shared `build` cache.

Explains the effect on branch A: on A's next run, GitLab restores the shared cache B just overwrote, so A's `node_modules/` is missing the package even though A's own lockfile still declares it and A never touched its lockfile.
Names the general failure mode — the shared fixed-key cache lets any branch clobber every other branch's dependency state, i.e. cross-branch cache contamination.
Provides the rewrite: change the cache key to be derived from the lockfile's content, e.g. `cache: key: files: [package-lock.json], paths: [node_modules/]`.
Explains why the fix isolates branches: GitLab hashes `package-lock.json`'s content into the key, so branches with different lockfiles land on distinct, non-overwriting caches.
Explains why the fix preserves performance: an unchanged lockfile still produces the same hash/key, so repeated runs still hit the cache (no loss of the speed benefit).

Gives a verification plan: run A's and B's pipelines in parallel with different lockfiles, check each job's cache log prints a different key, and confirm each branch's `node_modules/` matches its own lockfile regardless of run order.

Names Problem 1 as a migration-ordering issue: the diagram runs `ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL` before/independent of the canary rollout, while Stable v1 (95% of traffic) is still deployed and still writing to the same database.
Names Problem 2 as a sticky-session issue: session affinity pins a given user to one Pod for their whole session, rather than letting traffic be split per request.

Explains the causal mechanism of Problem 1: because v1's code has no value to write for the new NOT NULL column, its inserts fail immediately — and since v1 carries 95% of traffic, the outage hits nearly ALL users, not just the intended 5% canary.

Explains a causal mechanism of Problem 2: because pinning happens per-session (not per-request), a user stuck on the canary Pod is exposed to a canary bug for their entire session (bigger blast radius) and/or the measured 5% split no longer reflects the real request ratio.

Proposes the expand-contract fix for Problem 1: first 'expand' by adding the column as NULLABLE or with a DEFAULT so v1 and v2 can both write concurrently; only 'contract' to a true NOT NULL constraint in a later release once 100% of traffic is on v2.

Proposes a concrete fix for Problem 2: make the app stateless by moving session state to an external store (e.g. Redis) so the load balancer can route by request; if that can't be done in time, explicitly flags the measured canary percentage as unreliable and considers delaying the canary.

States the overall conclusion that both problems must be fixed (or their risk explicitly and knowingly accepted) before the canary as diagrammed can be trusted — not just two independent fixes, but a precondition on the whole plan.
build job (stage: build) runs a script that produces the dist/ output and declares it via artifacts.paths, so it becomes a build artifact available to later stages

unit_test and lint both declare needs: [build] only (not needing each other), so under GitLab's DAG scheduling they start as soon as build finishes, without waiting on each other or on the rest of the test stage
deploy_prod is gated by rules: if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"', the correct condition for a regular branch pipeline (as opposed to a merge request pipeline, where this variable could be empty)
deploy_prod declares needs: [unit_test, lint], guaranteeing it only starts after BOTH jobs have finished, not just one of them

deploy_prod uses $DEPLOY_TOKEN directly inside the deploy command (./deploy.sh --token "$DEPLOY_TOKEN") without echoing it or writing it to any file/log, so GitLab's project-level masked-variable setting hides it in the console output with no leak path

trigger_smoke_test declares needs: [deploy_prod], ensuring the child smoke-test pipeline is only triggered after deploy_prod has finished, matching the prompt's "after deploying, trigger..." requirement
trigger_smoke_test uses trigger: include: .../strategy: depend, the parent-child pipeline mechanism, explicitly different from needs (which only links jobs within the same pipeline)
strategy: depend makes the parent job wait on the child pipeline (smoke tests) and adopt its result to determine the parent job's own pass/fail status
Không đồng ý với đề xuất "quick and simple" dùng static IAM access key/secret key — đây chính là anti-pattern kinh điển của CI/CD vì key này không tự hết hạn.
Nếu key bị lộ (in ra log lỡ tay, workflow chạy trên fork PR, hoặc lỡ commit vào lịch sử), kẻ tấn công giữ quyền truy cập AWS VĨNH VIỄN cho đến khi ai đó chủ động xoay vòng key.
Việc xoay vòng key thủ công trong thực tế rất dễ bị quên, khiến rủi ro treo lơ lửng không có điểm dừng tự nhiên.
OIDC federation giải quyết đúng vấn đề này bằng cách thay static access key hoàn toàn bằng một JWT NGẮN HẠN mà GitHub Actions ký, đại diện cho workflow đang chạy.
AWS xác thực chữ ký của token đó qua cơ chế AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, tin tưởng GitHub như một IdP đã đăng ký.
AWS sau đó cấp một bộ credential tạm thời chỉ sống tối đa vài giờ (mặc định 1h, tối đa theo MaxSessionDuration của role).
Kết quả: không còn static secret nào tồn tại trong GitHub Secrets để bị lộ; và nếu một token cũ nào đó bị lộ ra (ví dụ trong debug log), nó hoàn toàn vô dụng vì đã hết hạn (exp) từ lâu.
Chính vì vậy OIDC federation là chuẩn bắt buộc cho mọi pipeline keyless hiện đại, thay vì "quick and simple" bằng static access key.
